feature.indexTitle: Nine features that talk to each other.
feature.indexLead: Training, food, cardio and community connected by the same progress. Open any of them to see how it works before you create an account.
feature.training.name: Guided training
feature.training.card: Phase-based guided programs, free sessions and a catalog of 1,578 exercises you can filter by equipment and muscle.
feature.training.metaDesc: A phased program with your week already laid out and a session that walks you set by set, with timed rest and 1,578 exercises to pick from.
feature.training.h1: Open the app. Today's session is already set.
feature.training.heroLead: You pick a program once and the app takes care of the rest: it splits your week into push, pull, legs and mobility days, and each day walks you set by set with the rest timed. All you have to do is show up.
feature.training.heroAlt: Today's workout screen: phase, weekday, exercise count, estimated duration and a start button.
feature.training.pathTitle: From the first screen to your first workout
feature.training.pathLead: You do not need to know which routine to pick or how to lay out your week.
feature.training.path1Desc: Your level, what you want to focus on (strength, pull-ups, handstand, full body…) and which days of the week you can train.
feature.training.path2Desc: The catalog surfaces the one that fits your level and your goal, with clear warnings if it asks for a lot of days, needs equipment or is worth checking with your doctor first.
feature.training.path3Desc: Every day with its type and its exercises: push, pull, legs, lower back, mobility and rest. And if on a Tuesday you feel like leg day, you train leg day — the calendar is not in charge.
feature.training.path4Desc: Today shows up at the top with its exercises and its estimated duration. One tap on START and the session takes over.
feature.training.pathLimit: Programs are split into phases that ramp up in difficulty, but moving to the next phase is your call, and today it is done from the web.
feature.training.sessTitle: What happens when you hit START
feature.training.sessLead: The screen holds one thing at a time. This is what you will see, in order.
feature.training.sess1Desc: The exercise name fills the screen, with its reps, the muscles it works and a dot for each set you have done. If you have done it before, it reminds you how many reps you managed last time and suggests one more. If the exercise has a note or a tempo, they show up right there.
feature.training.sess1Actions: Log the set · Edit reps, added weight, effort and note · Open the tutorial · Skip to the next exercise
feature.training.sess2Desc: A ring counts down and tells you what is coming next and which set you are on. It chimes at ten seconds and ticks for the last three. If you add or remove time, the app keeps that rest for that exercise and starts there next time.
feature.training.sess2Actions: −15 s · +15 s · +30 s · Skip the rest
feature.training.sess3Desc: Sessions come in three blocks. When the warm-up is done the app says so and lets you move into the main block; at the end it offers the stretches, which you can skip if you are in a hurry.
feature.training.sess4Title: How it went, in one line
feature.training.sess4Desc: Before closing it shows you the summary — title, sets and minutes — and lets you jot down how you felt. A month from now that line is worth more than any chart.
feature.training.sess5Title: And done: see where your time went
feature.training.sess5Desc: When you finish you get the breakdown of how long each exercise took, longest first, any records you broke and a card ready to send to the group chat.
feature.training.sess5Actions: Share the session · Back to your day
feature.training.sessNote: If you leave halfway through, the session waits for you: when you come back you pick up at the exact set you were on, even from the other device.
feature.training.sessOutro: Everything you log during the session — sets, reps, added weight and minutes — ends up in {{link}}, where it turns into your history, your records and your streaks.
feature.training.sess1Alt: Exercise screen during a session, with the reps, the set dots and the reminder of what you did last time.
feature.training.sess2Alt: Rest screen with the countdown ring, the next exercise announced and the buttons to adjust the time.
feature.training.sess5Alt: Final session screen with the breakdown of how long each exercise took.
feature.training.catTitle: What is inside, without rounding up
feature.training.catLead: The whole catalog ships inside the Android app, so you can search it even with no signal.
feature.training.cat1Desc: Exercises in the catalog, each with its description, the muscles it works and the equipment it needs.
feature.training.cat2Desc: Movement categories: push, pull, legs, core, lower back, full body, mobility and skills.
feature.training.cat3Desc: Equipment filters, starting with “no equipment”. You can see only what you can do today, with what you have.
feature.training.cat4Desc: Muscle groups to filter by when you want to work something specific.
feature.training.cat5Desc: Progression chains ordered by hand, from the easiest version to the hardest.
feature.training.cat6Desc: Exercises placed inside those chains, each with its own rule for moving up.
feature.training.cat7Desc: Steps in the pull-up chain, from hanging off the bar to the one-arm pull-up.
feature.training.catLimit: Most of the catalog comes from open exercise databases; what is curated by hand are the progression chains and the execution notes. Each exercise opens a tutorial on YouTube: the videos are not hosted in the app, and only a handful of exercises have an image of their own.
feature.training.catOffline: Browsing the catalog with no signal is a native-app thing; what does and does not get saved when you lose connection is covered in {{link}}.
feature.training.progTitle: How you know it is time to step up
feature.training.progLead: Two mechanisms, and both are concrete numbers instead of feelings.
feature.training.prog1Title: One more rep than last time
feature.training.prog1Desc: As soon as an exercise has history, the first set reminds you what you did last time and suggests one more rep. If you did it with added weight, it suggests 2.5 kg more. It works with any exercise you have ever logged.
feature.training.prog2Title: The next step in the chain
feature.training.prog2Desc: Catalog exercises that belong to a chain have a rep target. When you hit it in three sessions in a row, the “ready to advance” badge shows up along with the next exercise, one notch harder.
feature.training.progTableTitle: The bar rises with the level
feature.training.prog1Reps: 15 reps in 3 sessions in a row
feature.training.prog2Reps: 12 reps in 3 sessions in a row
feature.training.prog3Reps: 10 reps in 3 sessions in a row
feature.training.prog4Reps: 8 reps in 3 sessions in a row
feature.training.progLimit: Chains work with catalog exercises. Inside an official program the prompt you will see is the extra-rep one, which works on all of them.
feature.training.progOutro: The records you break along the way are saved automatically and live in {{link}}.
feature.training.progAlt: Exercise showing the ready-to-advance badge and the steps of its progression chain.
feature.training.ownTitle: When the plan does not fit
feature.training.ownLead: A program is a helping hand, not a sentence. There are three ways out.
feature.training.own1Desc: You pick whichever exercises you want from the catalog and the app works out what kind of day it is from the muscles you chose, so it can suggest a warm-up and stretches already timed. When you finish it is saved as a template you can repeat with one tap.
feature.training.own2Desc: You trained at the park without pulling your phone out: log the workout by hand, with its date, and it still counts towards your history and your streak.
feature.training.own3Desc: The editor walks you through four steps — info, phases, days and exercises — and fills in the warm-up on its own based on the day type. You can also duplicate an official program and tweak it to suit you.
feature.training.ownLimit: Logging a workout with a past date and sharing a program by link are web-only for now. And opening a shared program requires an account.
feature.training.ownCircuits: If what you are after is working in rounds and against the clock instead of by sets, that lives separately: see {{link}}.
feature.training.platLead: Training works on both. What changes is the setup, which is more comfortable on the web, and the company during the session, which is better on the phone.
feature.training.plat1: Pick a program and train the guided session
feature.training.plat2: Resume the session on the other device
feature.training.plat3: See every phase and the exercises of each day
feature.training.plat4: Log sets outside the guided session
feature.training.plat5: Log the set from the notification, with the phone locked
feature.training.plat6: Search the full catalog with no connection
feature.training.plat8: Move the program to another phase
feature.training.plat9: Log a workout with a past date
feature.training.platNote: The Android app is installed from the direct download. There is no published iOS version yet, so that column stays empty even though the code is the same.
feature.training.faq1q: Does it work if I have never trained?
feature.training.faq1a: Yes. Beginner programs start with push-ups — and the note tells you to do them from your knees if full ones are not there yet — and with the Australian row, done on a low bar with your feet on the ground. On top of that, most movements have an easier version to fall back on.
feature.training.faq2q: Do I need a bar or a gym?
feature.training.faq2a: Not to start. You can filter the catalog by the equipment you have, starting with “no equipment”, and see only the exercises you can do today. A bar, parallel bars, rings or added weight open up more, but they are not the starting point.
feature.training.faq3q: Do I have to train on the day the program says?
feature.training.faq3a: No. The week is a guide: you can open any day and train it whenever you want. Today is marked, but nothing forces you to follow it.
feature.training.faq4q: What if I get interrupted halfway through a session?
feature.training.faq4a: The session saves itself with every set. You can leave, do something else and come back to the exact set you were on, even from the other device if you started on the computer and continue on your phone.
feature.training.faq5q: Can I create my own program?
feature.training.faq5a: Yes, with the four-step editor, on the web and on your phone: you define the phases, the days and the exercises of each day. You can also duplicate an official program and change it. Sharing it with someone by link is done from the web, and whoever opens it will need an account.
feature.training.faq6a: The exercise catalog ships inside the Android app, so you can browse it with no data. Logging your sets does need a connection to save to your account: {{link}} explains what holds up and what does not.
feature.nutrition.name: Nutrition and pantry
feature.nutrition.card: Meal logging, macros, an AI pantry, saved recipes and a shopping list with cost per meal.
feature.nutrition.metaDesc: Log meals from a photo, track macros and water, keep your pantry up to date and build the shopping list with prices taken from your own purchases.
feature.nutrition.h1: From what is in your kitchen to what you eat today
feature.nutrition.heroLead: You log the meal, the app offers to take it out of your pantry, and whatever runs out shows up on the shopping list by itself. This is not a calorie counter: it is the whole loop, and it closes.
feature.nutrition.heroBadge: Photo or text · macros and water · pantry and shopping list
feature.nutrition.heroAlt: The day at a glance: calorie ring, protein, carb and fat bars, and one logged meal with its time, its quality grade and its cost.
feature.nutrition.loopLead: Five steps that bite their own tail. Start anywhere and the rest falls into place.
feature.nutrition.loop1Desc: A photo of the plate, a written sentence, or two taps if it is something you eat often. Calories, macros, the time and the photo all get saved.
feature.nutrition.loop2Title: The app offers to take it out
feature.nutrition.loop2Desc: Right after, it asks whether to subtract those ingredients from your pantry, matching what you wrote with what you have: "grilled chicken breast" with your "chicken", and 250 grams with your kilo and a half.
feature.nutrition.loop3Title: The inventory goes down on its own
feature.nutrition.loop3Desc: Your pantry shows what is actually left, not what you bought three weeks ago. Whatever runs out gets flagged, and whatever has sat untouched for a while loses confidence and gets questioned.
feature.nutrition.loop4Desc: With what ran out, what expires before your next shop and what your plan calls for. Every line carries its reason and an estimated price based on what you paid last time.
feature.nutrition.loop5Desc: And everything you bought lands in the pantry with its price, merged with what was already there. Back to step one.
feature.nutrition.loopNote: Every step goes through a screen you can edit first. The AI proposes; what gets saved is your call.
feature.nutrition.loopOutro: And because every meal is timestamped, the loop feeds {{link}}: the calendar, the charts and the weekly summary.
feature.nutrition.waysTitle: Six ways to log a meal
feature.nutrition.waysLead: Because a home-cooked plate, a packaged product and your usual breakfast are not the same problem.
feature.nutrition.way1When: Home cooking or a restaurant. You can upload up to five photos and add a note for context.
feature.nutrition.way2When: "200 g of grilled chicken with brown rice and a bit of avocado." No photo, just as complete.
feature.nutrition.way3When: You know the name and want values from a record rather than an estimate.
feature.nutrition.way4When: Packaged product: point the camera at the code and its values come back.
feature.nutrition.way5When: The usual breakfast. Your most frequent meals are one tap away, and you can save templates.
feature.nutrition.way6When: You already know the numbers and just want to write them down, with nobody estimating anything.
feature.nutrition.waysNote: Analysing a photo can take a moment, because it goes looking for real data. If you are in a hurry there is a button to let it finish in the background and ping you when it is done.
feature.nutrition.aiTitle: What happens when you hit analyse
feature.nutrition.aiLead: It is not a photo in and a number out.
feature.nutrition.ai1Desc: It identifies the foods on the plate and queries a public product database for their values per hundred grams. If something is not there, it searches the web before estimating it.
feature.nutrition.ai2Title: The numbers have to add up
feature.nutrition.ai2Desc: When it finishes, a calculation checks that the calories match the protein, carbs and fat. If they drift too far apart, they get recomputed from the macros.
feature.nutrition.ai3Desc: It is asked to estimate using visual references —the size of the plate, your palm, your fist— and to explain how it reached each portion. A medium steak weighs 185 grams, not "200".
feature.nutrition.aiScore: Every meal gets a grade from A to E, and the model assigns it knowing your goal, the macros you have left for the day and the time you ate. The daily grade is the average of your meals weighted by calories: with fewer than two graded meals there is no grade for the day yet.
feature.nutrition.aiLimit: It is still an estimate, and you can correct any value before saving. A meal's quality grade is guidance to help you see patterns, not medical advice or a clinical nutrition plan. If you have a health condition, talk to a professional.
feature.nutrition.goalLead: From a well-known formula over your weight, height, age and how much you move. Then it is adjusted for what you are after.
feature.nutrition.goal1Effect: You add around 300 kcal over your expenditure and protein goes up to 2 g per kilo.
feature.nutrition.goal2Effect: You cut around 500 kcal and protein goes up to 2.2 g per kilo so you do not lose muscle along the way.
feature.nutrition.goal3Effect: A small deficit, around 200 kcal, with protein kept high.
feature.nutrition.goal4Effect: You stay at your estimated expenditure, with 1.8 g of protein per kilo.
feature.nutrition.goalPace: You also pick the pace —gradual, balanced or aggressive— and the adjustment gets softer or sharper. Before applying the change you see how your numbers would end up.
feature.nutrition.goalAuto: If you leave your targets on automatic they recompute themselves when your weight, height or activity level changes. If you prefer to set them by hand, they are never touched. Water is tracked separately, with its own target and glass shortcuts.
feature.nutrition.goalLimit: The numbers are a statistical estimate, not a prescription: if you have a health condition or follow medical guidance, that one wins. And when you switch {{link}} the app tells you in case you want to recompute, but it does not do it on its own.
feature.nutrition.moneyTitle: What eating like this costs you
feature.nutrition.moneyLead: No artificial intelligence computes this part: it is your prices and a subtraction.
feature.nutrition.money1Desc: When you write down what you paid for something, the app keeps that price per kilo or per unit and uses it to estimate what your next shopping list will cost.
feature.nutrition.money2Title: Every meal can carry its cost
feature.nutrition.money2Desc: If the ingredients came out of your pantry, that meal's card shows what it cost. And the day shows total spend and the average per meal.
feature.nutrition.money3Desc: You photograph the supermarket receipt and the products, the store and the date get read off it. If the receipt has the exchange rate printed on it, that is the one used: so a history in another currency does not fall apart when the rate moves.
feature.nutrition.moneyLimit: If you have never bought something, that line comes out with no price. If the pantry only covered part of the meal, you will see an "at least" in front of the figure. The app does not invent prices and does not query any market price database: it only knows what you have told it.
feature.nutrition.moneyOutro: One caveat: the maths runs on the server. Logging a meal, writing to the pantry or generating a list all need a connection — the only thing that survives {{link}} in nutrition is your glasses of water.
feature.nutrition.platTitle: What you can do in each place
feature.nutrition.platLead: Logging, the pantry and the shopping list work the same in both. Two logging shortcuts are still web only.
feature.nutrition.plat1: Log by photo, by text, by repeating or by hand
feature.nutrition.plat2: The day's macros, calories and water
feature.nutrition.plat6: Shopping list with prices and "shopping done"
feature.nutrition.platNote: The Android app installs from the direct download. There is no published iOS version yet: on iPhone you use it from the browser.
feature.nutrition.faq1q: Do I have to weigh everything?
feature.nutrition.faq1a: No. You can log by servings or by units, and when you estimate from a photo it uses visual references —the size of the plate, your palm— instead of asking you for a scale. What matters is the trend across the week, not the exact number on a Tuesday.
feature.nutrition.faq2q: Does it work with food from my country?
feature.nutrition.faq2a: Yes. You can describe the dish in your own words and with your own names, or photograph it. On the web you can also search the food by name or scan the barcode of a packaged product.
feature.nutrition.faq3q: Does the AI decide my diet?
feature.nutrition.faq3a: No. It proposes values and recipes, and you confirm or correct before anything is saved. The estimates and the meal grades are guidance to help you see patterns, not medical advice or a clinical plan.
feature.nutrition.faq4a: So the app knows what you have at home. With that it suggests recipes from what is already in the kitchen, tells you how many meals you can cover and which ingredient limits you, and builds the shopping list from what ran out or is about to expire.
feature.nutrition.faq5q: Where do the prices come from?
feature.nutrition.faq5a: From you. When you write down what you paid —by hand or by photographing the receipt— the app stores that price and uses it to estimate the cost of your next purchases and your meals. There is no supermarket price database behind it.
feature.nutrition.faq6a: Glasses of water are saved offline and sync when you are back. Logging meals, writing to the pantry or generating a list all need a connection.

feature.progress.name: Progress and insights
feature.progress.card: Unified calendar, per-exercise charts, progress photos, records and a weekly summary.
feature.progress.metaDesc: A calendar that crosses eleven signals a day, charts of your best sets, before-and-after photos and a weekly summary that looks for patterns.
feature.progress.h1: Your whole month, on one screen
feature.progress.heroLead: Workouts, cardio, meals, sleep, weight, measurements and photos, all in the same calendar. Tap a day and see exactly what happened. And at the end of the week, a summary that looks for the relationship between one thing and another.
feature.progress.heroBadge: Eleven signals a day · automatic records · weekly summary
feature.progress.calTitle: Eleven signals, a month at a glance
feature.progress.calLead: Every point on a day is something you logged. Here is the full list.
feature.progress.cal1Source: Your program's session for the day, once you complete it.
feature.progress.cal2Source: Workouts you put together yourself, outside the plan.
feature.progress.cal3Source: Runs, walks and bike rides with GPS.
feature.progress.cal5Source: How many you logged and the day's calories.
feature.progress.cal7Source: The hours and quality of the night.
feature.progress.cal8Source: Every time you weigh yourself and write it down.
feature.progress.cal9Source: The days you get out the tape measure.
feature.progress.cal11Source: How your back feels, from one to five.
feature.progress.calDay: Tapping a day opens what happened: your sessions, linked to their detail, plus everything else you logged. And if you did not train that day, it shows you what your program had planned.
feature.progress.calResilience: The calendar pulls each thing from a different place. If one of them fails to load, the month still renders with everything else instead of going blank.
feature.progress.strTitle: What gets measured and what it means
feature.progress.strLead: Four charts and a calculator over the same thing, so you know whether you are progressing or repeating.
feature.progress.str1Means: Your best set from each session, over time. Points in another colour are free sessions.
feature.progress.str2What: Load over the last few weeks
feature.progress.str2Means: Everything your sets moved over four weeks, with the change from the previous one.
feature.progress.str3Means: How many sets your program has planned for each group this week, so you can see if something is falling short.
feature.progress.str4Means: How the added weight on a given exercise has climbed.
feature.progress.str5Means: Your estimated max from a real set, with the percentage table to plan around.
feature.progress.prDesc: Nothing to mark: every time you open the app it goes through your whole set history and rebuilds your best mark for each exercise. It reads reps the way you write them — “8-12” counts as twelve — and if the exercise carried added weight, the record is in kilos.
feature.progress.prCelebrate: When you break one, the app celebrates it on the spot and lets you send the card to whoever you want.
feature.progress.strLimit: The charts and the calculator are in the web version. The estimated max is exactly that, an estimate from a formula, and if you have never logged your body weight the calculator starts from a default figure: log your weight once and the numbers come out with yours.
feature.progress.bodyTitle: What the scale alone does not tell you
feature.progress.bodyLead: Four logs you can keep side by side, and that cross-reference each other.
feature.progress.body1Desc: You log it when you weigh yourself and see the curve, the current figure, the lowest, the highest and where the trend is heading.
feature.progress.body2Desc: Chest, waist, neck, hips, both arms and both thighs, with a tape measure. Every time you take them they are compared against the previous time. You do not need to fill in all of them.
feature.progress.body3Desc: It is estimated from your circumferences, with its category and your lean mass, and the trend gets charted. It is usually what explains why the weight is not dropping but your clothes fit better.
feature.progress.body4Desc: Front, side and back, sorted by date, with a slider to overlay two of them and see the real difference.
feature.progress.bodyLimit: Body-fat percentage is estimated with a tape measure and has a margin of three or four points: it is good for seeing the trend, not as a clinical value. To compare two photos on the web they need to be the same view. And weight, today, gets logged from the web or by syncing a watch.
feature.progress.weekLead: Once a week, all your logs get looked at together, looking for what goes with what.
feature.progress.week1Desc: Sleep, workouts, meals, water, weight and measurements from the last seven days, compared against the seven before that. On Android, if you have a watch connected, also steps and heart rate.
feature.progress.week2Desc: A headline, whether you are improving or dropping off, the relationships it finds with their confidence level, what went well, what is worth watching and one concrete suggestion with a button that takes you straight to doing it.
feature.progress.week3Desc: It needs at least three days of data in the week. With notifications on it arrives by itself on Monday morning; if not, you request it with a button whenever you feel like it.
feature.progress.weekLimit: These are patterns observed in your own logs: no causes, no diagnoses, no medical advice. When a metric has too few days, it gets marked as insufficient and nothing is claimed about it, and weak relationships get set aside as “possible patterns” instead of being sold as findings.
feature.progress.privTitle: What is private and what is not
feature.progress.privLead: This is where photos of your body get stored, so we spell it out in full instead of summing it up as “only you”.
feature.progress.priv1Who: Only your account. They are not shared with anyone and do not show up on any feed.
feature.progress.priv5What: Your pull-up, push-up, L-sit, pistol squat and handstand records
feature.progress.priv5Who: Other people with an account can see these: they are what feeds the leaderboard and the challenges.
feature.progress.priv6Who: Anyone with an account can look them up; in the activity feed they show for the people who follow you.
feature.progress.privLimit: A technical note we would rather say out loud: your photos are only listed for your account, but the file itself is served from a long, hard-to-guess address; anyone who got hold of that exact address could open it. Do not upload anything you would not post if that address ever leaked.
feature.progress.platTitle: What you can do on each platform
feature.progress.platLead: The calendar, the photos and the summary work on both. The charts and the calculator, for now, are on the web.
feature.progress.plat1: Unified calendar with each day's detail
feature.progress.plat4: Records with celebration and a shareable card
feature.progress.plat6: Charts by exercise, load and muscle group
feature.progress.plat9: Exporting sessions and weight to CSV
feature.progress.plat10: Sharing the transformation as an image
feature.progress.platNote: The Android app installs from the direct download. There is no published iOS version yet: on iPhone you use it from the browser.
feature.progress.faq1q: How long until I see something?
feature.progress.faq1a: An exercise chart opens up once you have two sessions with logged reps. The weekly summary needs at least three days of data. The calendar, on the other hand, starts filling in from your very first log.
feature.progress.faq2q: Who can see my progress photos?
feature.progress.faq2a: Only you. Photos, measurements, weight, sleep and your summaries are private to your account. What other people do see are your pull-up, push-up and other records, because they feed the leaderboard and the challenges, plus your completed workouts, which anyone with an account can look up and which show in the feed of whoever follows you.
feature.progress.faq3q: Is the weekly summary medical advice?
feature.progress.faq3a: No. These are patterns observed in your own logs, with no causes or diagnoses, meant as a hint for your next adjustment. If you have a health condition, your healthcare professional is the one who decides.
feature.progress.faq4q: Do I have to log my weight and measurements for it to be useful?
feature.progress.faq4a: No. Workouts, sets, cardio and meals save themselves as you log them. Weight, measurements and photos are ones you log whenever you want: they are the ones that best tell the changes the scale does not explain.
feature.progress.faq5q: Can I get my data out of the app?
feature.progress.faq5a: From the web you can download your sessions with their sets, and your weight history, as CSV. Measurements, photos and summaries do not export yet.
feature.progress.faq6a: It is an estimate based on circumferences, with a margin of three or four points. It is good for seeing where the trend is heading if you take the measurements the same way each time, not as a clinical value.

feature.cardio.name: GPS cardio
feature.cardio.card: Running, walking and cycling with live GPS, a route map and a shareable session card.
feature.cardio.metaTitle: GPS cardio: route, pace and splits
feature.cardio.metaDesc: Track running, walking or cycling with GPS: route on the map, pace, splits and elevation. On Android it keeps recording with the screen locked.
feature.cardio.h1: Your route on the map, kilometre by kilometre.
feature.cardio.heroLead: Running, walking and cycling with GPS: distance, pace, splits and elevation while you move. On Android the session keeps recording with the screen locked, and you can pause it from the notification without unlocking the phone.
feature.cardio.heroBadge: Android · keeps recording in the background
feature.cardio.shot1Alt: Detail of a running session: the route drawn on the map with distance, duration and average pace.
feature.cardio.measureTitle: What it measures, and where each number comes from
feature.cardio.measureLead: None of this is a marketing estimate: every number follows a rule, and here they all are.
feature.cardio.m1Source: Distance between GPS points smoothed with a Kalman filter.
feature.cardio.m1Note: Fixes with accuracy worse than 20 m are dropped, and so is any movement under 3 m: standing still, the kilometres do not go up.
feature.cardio.m2Source: The speed field reported by the GPS, only above 0.5 m/s.
feature.cardio.m2Note: It is the device instant speed, not distance over time: that is why it reacts fast on hills.
feature.cardio.m3Source: One per full kilometre, plus a partial one if more than 100 m are left at the end.
feature.cardio.m3Note: The partial split is normalised to min/km so you can compare it with the rest.
feature.cardio.m4Source: The sum of every altitude increase the GPS reports.
feature.cardio.m4Note: No barometer and no smoothing: treat it as a rough figure, not a precise one.
feature.cardio.m5Source: The fastest 200 m stretch of the whole session.
feature.cardio.m5Note: It is not "your best kilometre": it is a 200 m sliding window.
feature.cardio.m6Source: A three-point moving average over the GPS speed.
feature.cardio.m6Note: That way a single bad fix does not gift you a sprint you never ran.
feature.cardio.m7Source: The activity MET × your weight × duration.
feature.cardio.m7Note: It is an estimate: in the same time, 3 km and 5 km give the same figure. With no weight on record it assumes 70 kg.
feature.cardio.m8Source: From your watch, via Health Connect, once the session is already saved.
feature.cardio.m8Note: Android only, and only if the time window matches. Never live.
feature.cardio.runTitle: You start it, pocket the phone and the session carries on
feature.cardio.runLead: This is a full session in the Android app, from the start button to the shareable card.
feature.cardio.run1Desc: One button and you are recording. If today is a cardio day in your program, the screen says so and it gets marked as done when you finish.
feature.cardio.run2Desc: The split in progress, GPS accuracy with a traffic light and the map drawing itself underneath as you go.
feature.cardio.run3Desc: Kilometres and pace kept up to date, a stopwatch that runs on its own and a button to pause without unlocking the phone. If the system kills the app, the session picks up where it was when you reopen it.
feature.cardio.run4Title: Map, splits and a card to send
feature.cardio.run4Desc: Full route, elevation profile, calories, elevation gain and best pace, the splits table and room for your note. The card with your route takes one tap.
feature.cardio.runKmHaptic: Every completed kilometre gives you a vibration: with the phone in your pocket it is the only cue that gets through.
feature.cardio.runOutro: Cardio counts like any other workout: it shows up in your activity, in your calendar and in {{link}}.
feature.cardio.actTitle: Running, walking and riding are not measured the same
feature.cardio.actLead: The app changes the units, the route colour and the plausibility thresholds depending on what you are doing.
feature.cardio.actNote: On a bike the whole session switches from min/km to km/h. And snapping the route to the streets, which only exists on the web, uses the driving profile: the public routing service has no cycling profile.
feature.cardio.gapTitle: When the GPS fails, we tell you
feature.cardio.gapLead: A tunnel, a building, your pocket. Losing signal happens: what changes is what the app does next.
feature.cardio.gapBeforeDesc: Join the two ends of the gap with a straight line and hand you those kilometres as if you had run them.
feature.cardio.gapAfterDesc: It marks the stretch as a gap after 30 seconds without signal, draws it dashed on the map and only adds that distance if the implied speed is plausible for your activity. If the track is not clean, the kilometres show a tilde and a warning with how many gaps there were.
feature.cardio.qualityGoodDesc: Not a single gap and at least 10 points per kilometre. The numbers stand as they are.
feature.cardio.qualityEstimatedDesc: There was a gap, or fewer than 10 points per kilometre. Distance is shown as approximate.
feature.cardio.qualityPoorDesc: More than 20% of the distance comes from gaps, or fewer than 3 points per kilometre. Warning in red.
feature.cardio.gapLimit: If no fix has come in after 15 seconds, the app restarts the GPS on its own. And if it is the connection that fails, the session is kept on the phone and uploaded when it can — with two limits worth knowing: the queue holds 5 unsent sessions and an active session expires after 24 hours. More on {{link}}.
feature.cardio.platTitle: What changes depending on where you use it
feature.cardio.platLead: The web records with GPS as long as you keep it open, and on top of that it snaps the route to the streets and exports GPX. The Android app is the one that survives a locked screen.
feature.cardio.p2: Keeps recording with the screen locked
feature.cardio.p3: Notification with metrics and a stopwatch
feature.cardio.p4: Pause and resume from the notification
feature.cardio.p6: Map, elevation profile and splits table
feature.cardio.p8: Export GPX of the session you just finished
feature.cardio.p9: Heart rate and calories from your watch
feature.cardio.p10: Home screen widget with the week kilometres
feature.cardio.p12: Saved if the connection fails, recovered if the app closes
feature.cardio.platNote: There is no iPhone app yet, and the Android one installs as an APK: it is not on Google Play.
feature.cardio.limitTitle: What it still does not do
feature.cardio.limit1: There is no iPhone app. On iOS you cannot record in the background and there is no build to install.
feature.cardio.limit2: On the web the GPS only records with the tab open and visible: it is not a replacement for the app when you head outside.
feature.cardio.limit3: There is no auto-pause, no pace alerts, no manual laps and no cardio intervals.
feature.cardio.limit4: There is no live heart rate, no Bluetooth sensors and no cadence.
feature.cardio.limit5: You cannot plan routes or follow a route loaded beforehand.
feature.cardio.limit6: GPX is exported from the web only, and only for the session you just finished. There is no import, no Strava and no Garmin.
feature.cardio.limit7: A session link asks for an account to open: to send it to someone outside, use the card.
feature.cardio.fq1: Does it really keep recording with the phone in my pocket?
feature.cardio.fa1: On Android it does: the session runs in a foreground service with a persistent notification, so the system does not cut it off and you can pause it from the lock screen. On the web it does not: if you lock the phone or switch apps, the browser suspends the page.
feature.cardio.fa2: Quite a bit more than a strength session: the GPS asks for a position every second in navigation mode and the screen stays on during the session. We do not quote percentages because we have not measured them properly.
feature.cardio.fq3: What happens if I lose signal or the app closes?
feature.cardio.fa3: Losing signal opens a gap: it is drawn dashed and that distance only counts if it is plausible. If the app closes, the session is restored from a save made every 5 seconds. And with no connection it stays on the phone and uploads later — the queue holds 5 sessions and an active session expires after 24 hours.
feature.cardio.fq4: Do races against friends use this same GPS?
feature.cardio.fa4: No. {{link}} have their own tracking, more forgiving and simpler: it only adds distance inside the competition time window, with no splits and no elevation.
feature.cardio.fq5: Can I take my data with me?
feature.cardio.fa5: From the web you can download the GPX of the session you just finished. Exporting the full history or syncing with Strava or Garmin is not there yet.
feature.circuits.name: Circuits and HIIT
feature.circuits.card: Round-based circuits and timed blocks, with templates and configurable rests.
feature.circuits.metaTitle: Circuits and HIIT with a timer
feature.circuits.metaDesc: Train by rounds or by work and rest intervals, with a full-screen countdown, audio cues and every timing under your control.
feature.circuits.heroLead: You pick the exercises, set the rounds and the timings, and the app takes care of the clock: a full-screen countdown, a cue before every change and nothing to read while you move.
feature.circuits.heroBadge: Two modes · 1 to 20 rounds · 10 to 120 s of work
feature.circuits.heroAlt: Full-screen countdown in the work phase, showing the current round and the next exercise
feature.circuits.modeLead: Same screen, two ways to keep the pace. You choose before you start.
feature.circuits.mode1Circuit: You: you tap when you finish each exercise.
feature.circuits.mode1Timed: The clock: every block lasts exactly what you set.
feature.circuits.mode2Circuit: Chained sets by reps, strength work.
feature.circuits.mode2Timed: HIIT, Tabata and anything by intervals.
feature.circuits.mode3Circuit: The exercise, the reps you owe and a big done button.
feature.circuits.mode3Timed: The ring with the seconds left and the exercise in progress.
feature.circuits.mode4Circuit: Whenever you want: one tap moves you on.
feature.circuits.mode4Timed: Not during work; rest can be skipped.
feature.circuits.mode5Circuit: It depends on your pace, so there's no telling beforehand.
feature.circuits.mode5Timed: It's worked out for you and shown before you hit start.
feature.circuits.demoTitle: This is what you see while training
feature.circuits.demoLead: This is the real countdown, with the timings the app ships by default. Press play and watch it.
feature.circuits.demoStatic: The sequence goes: five seconds to get into position, forty of work and twenty of rest, then round and round until the rounds are done.
feature.circuits.demoAlt: Countdown ring showing the current phase and the seconds left
feature.circuits.demo1: It warns you with eleven seconds left and ticks on the last three, so you never have to look.
feature.circuits.demo2: The screen stays awake for as long as the circuit lasts.
feature.circuits.demo3: On Android the cues play even with the phone on silent, and they mix with your music instead of cutting it.
feature.circuits.demo4: You can pause and pick up where you left off by tapping anywhere on the screen.
feature.circuits.demo5: If the app closes by accident, coming back drops you into the circuit at the round you were on.
feature.circuits.demoLimit: The timer needs the app in front of you: there's still no tracking with the phone locked and no lock-screen notice. To head out with the phone in your pocket, use {{link}}.
feature.circuits.cfgLead: No hidden settings, no paid tier: these are all of them, with their limits.
feature.circuits.cfgZero: Zero counts as a decision, not a gap: set the rest between exercises to zero and the next one starts with no pause; set it between rounds and the next round starts without stopping.
feature.circuits.cfgPresets: The web version ships three starting points: Tabata (eight rounds of twenty seconds with ten of rest), EMOM (four rounds of one minute) and a bodyweight circuit of five exercises and three rounds. The first two are timing presets you add your own exercises to from {{link}}; the third comes complete. The Android app has no templates: you go in through Free session and build from scratch.
feature.circuits.cfgLimit: The settings go back to their defaults every time you come in: circuits can't be saved for later yet, and they can't be named. What does stay saved is the exact setup inside the circuit you finish.
feature.circuits.endLead: A finished circuit isn't a timer that switches off: it's one more session.
feature.circuits.end1Desc: It records how you did it —mode, rounds, work and rest timings and the list of exercises— along with how long it actually took. And you can leave a note about how it went.
feature.circuits.end2Title: It shows up in your calendar
feature.circuits.end2Desc: It appears in {{link}} on the day you did it, next to your workouts, your cardio and everything else you log.
feature.circuits.end3Desc: It adds to your workout total, moves your streak on the leaderboard, and whoever follows you gets the heads-up that you trained today.
feature.circuits.endLimit: Quit halfway and nothing is saved: the circuit is recorded when you reach the end. The full detail of a past circuit is viewed from the web. And there's still no list of your circuits or stats of their own for this feature: you see them month by month in the calendar.
feature.circuits.shot1Alt: Detail of a finished circuit with its rounds, its timings and the list of exercises
feature.circuits.platTitle: What you can do on each one
feature.circuits.platLead: The timer is identical on both. What changes is how you get in and what you can review afterwards.
feature.circuits.plat1: Build the circuit and pick mode, rounds and timings
feature.circuits.plat3: Pick the circuit back up if the app closes
feature.circuits.plat4: Save it even if you lose connection
feature.circuits.plat5: A screen of its own with starting templates
feature.circuits.plat6: View the detail of a finished circuit
feature.circuits.plat8: Heart rate and calories from a compatible watch
feature.circuits.platNote: The Android app is installed from the direct download. There's still no published iOS version: you use it from the browser.
feature.circuits.faq1q: Does it work for HIIT or Tabata?
feature.circuits.faq1a: Yes, that's what timed mode is for: blocks of work and rest repeated for as many rounds as you want. A classic Tabata —twenty seconds of work, ten of rest, eight rounds— fits as is, and on the web you have it as a starting point.
feature.circuits.faq2a: In circuit mode yes: one tap moves you to the next one. In timed mode the work block lasts what it lasts and can't be cut short, though you can skip the rest.
feature.circuits.faq3q: Does it count towards my stats?
feature.circuits.faq3a: Yes. A finished circuit adds to your session total, counts for the leaderboard, shows up in your calendar and tells your followers you trained. The streak you see on the home screen, for now, only looks at your workouts and your cardio.
feature.circuits.faq4q: Can I save a circuit to repeat it?
feature.circuits.faq4a: Not yet: the settings go back to their defaults every time. What you can do is open the circuit you finished and see exactly how you set it up, so you can rebuild it in a minute.
feature.circuits.faq5q: Can I lock the phone while I train?
feature.circuits.faq5a: No: the timer needs the app on screen, although the screen stays awake by itself for the whole circuit. To train with the phone put away, {{link}} does keep measuring.
feature.circuits.faq6q: What if the app closes halfway?
feature.circuits.faq6a: Opening it again drops you back into the circuit at the round you were on, for up to twenty-four hours. And if you finish with no connection, it's stored on the phone and uploaded on its own once it's back.
feature.races.name: Races
feature.races.card: Races with a lobby, a live distance board and shareable results.
feature.races.metaDesc: Create a race, share the link and everyone runs wherever they are: synced start, live GPS board and final results when the window closes.
feature.races.h1: Run together. From wherever you are.
feature.races.heroLead: A race is a shared time window: the creator starts it, everyone sets off on the same second and each phone’s GPS counts the kilometres. Nobody has to show up at the same park.
feature.races.heroAlt: Live race board with three runners and the remaining time
feature.races.lifeTitle: Four states, from the invite to the podium
feature.races.lifeLead: A race goes through four screens. Here is what every participant sees on each one, and what they can do.
feature.races.life1Desc: The race name and its target up top; below, the participant list growing live and who has already tapped Ready. Creating the race does not sign you up: the creator taps Join too. One participant is enough to start, because Ready blocks nothing.
feature.races.life1Actions: Join · Tap Ready (guests) · Share the link or show the QR · Start and Cancel, creator only
feature.races.life1Alt: Race lobby with three participants and the join button
feature.races.life2Desc: The creator starts the race and a full-screen countdown takes over, with a tick and a vibration. There is a single start time for the whole race, stored on the server: it is not a stopwatch per person.
feature.races.life2Actions: You can still join during the countdown; once it is running, you cannot
feature.races.life2Alt: Full-screen start countdown showing the number three in lime green
feature.races.life3Title: Your phone counts, the board reorders
feature.races.life3Desc: Kilometres, time —or what is left, if the race is on the clock— and pace up top; the progress bar towards the target; below, the standings and the map showing who is where. Your progress reaches everyone else every three seconds, and on the web a sound tells you when your position changes.
feature.races.life3Actions: Leave · Finish the race: on the web only the creator, on Android everyone sees the button
feature.races.life3Alt: Live race with your own stats, progress bar and standings
feature.races.life4Title: Podium, then straight to the group chat
feature.races.life4Desc: Who won, the race time and the full standings with the DNFs at the bottom. Anyone who leaves or falls short shows up as DNF, not with a half-finished distance. From here you can {{link}} so the race counts in your history.
feature.races.life4Actions: Save as workout · Export GPX and results card, web only
feature.races.life4Alt: Race results with the winner, the standings and one DNF participant
feature.races.lifeNote: There is a fifth state that is not shown above because nobody sees it: if the creator cancels before the start, the race closes and no result is recorded.
feature.races.linkTitle: One link and they are in
feature.races.linkLead: No codes and no private rooms to set up: a race is a web address you share.
feature.races.link1Desc: From the lobby anyone can copy the link, open the system share sheet or, on the web, show a QR code to be scanned with a phone camera.
feature.races.link2Desc: If you marked the race public, pasting the link into WhatsApp or Telegram shows a preview with the real name and target, generated by the server. If it is private, nothing leaks.
feature.races.link3Title: You need an account to see it
feature.races.link3Desc: The link is public, but whoever opens it without signing in only gets a login screen: no name, no target, no participants. Creating the account is free and takes a minute.
feature.races.linkLimit: You can get in until the last second of the countdown. Once the race is under way you cannot: a latecomer could not be ranked fairly.
feature.races.boardLead: The standings reorder while you run. These are the columns, and the rule that decides the winner.
feature.races.board1Desc: Current position. Those who finished first, then those still running, and the DNFs at the bottom.
feature.races.board2Desc: The name they joined with, with the leader mark and your own row highlighted in lime.
feature.races.board3Desc: Minutes per kilometre, computed from the distance and time each phone reports.
feature.races.board4Desc: Time in the race, measured against the server clock rather than the phone’s.
feature.races.board5Desc: Distance covered to two decimals, plus the coloured dot telling you whether they are still running or already done.
feature.races.rankTitle: Who wins, depending on the race type
feature.races.rank1Rule: Whoever completes the distance first: finish time decides.
feature.races.rank2Mode: On the clock, or with no target distance
feature.races.rank2Rule: Whoever covers the most distance. Ties break on pace, and then alphabetically, so the board does not jitter.
feature.races.rank3Rule: Anyone who leaves or falls short shows as DNF, always at the bottom of the board.
feature.races.robustTitle: Built for a park, not a laboratory
feature.races.robustLead: Patchy coverage, a phone with the wrong clock, a tab that reloads. Here is what the app does about it.
feature.races.robust1Desc: The start, your time and every point of your route are computed against the server clock, measured when you enter the race. Two phones with skewed clocks compete on equal terms.
feature.races.robust2Desc: GPS does not need data: your route keeps recording on the phone, and failed uploads retry after one second, three and nine. When the connection returns, your position catches up.
feature.races.robust3Desc: Every upload saves a local copy of your distance and your trace. Reload the page mid-race and it picks up from there instead of reporting zero kilometres.
feature.races.robust4Desc: Readings with more than 30 metres of error are ignored entirely, and jumps of more than 500 metres between two readings never count towards your distance.
feature.races.robustLimit: Three limits worth knowing before you bet anything on it. A race needs the app in the foreground with the screen on: there is no background tracking, that is what {{link}} is for. If someone loses coverage, everyone else sees them frozen at their last distance, with no warning. And closing the race is triggered by a phone with the screen open, not by the server: if everybody closes the app halfway, the race stays open.

feature.races.vsLead: A race is a time window with GPS. A challenge is a goal you accumulate against a deadline. If the problem is that you never manage to be free at the same hour, what you want is a challenge.

feature.races.vs5Challenge: Yes: you get a notification when someone joins your challenge

feature.races.faq1q: Do we have to run in the same place?
feature.races.faq1a: No. Everyone runs wherever they are; what you share is the time window. What gets compared is whatever each phone’s GPS measures inside that window.
feature.races.faq2a: It depends on the type. If you set a target distance, whoever completes it first wins. If the race is on the clock, or you set no distance, whoever covers the most kilometres wins, and pace breaks the tie.
feature.races.faq3q: What if I lose signal halfway?
feature.races.faq3a: GPS does not need data, so your route keeps recording and failed uploads retry on their own. Your position on the board catches up as soon as the connection is back. In the meantime everyone else sees you frozen at your last distance.
feature.races.faq4q: Can I join a race that already started?
feature.races.faq4a: You can get in until the last second of the countdown. Once it is running, no: a latecomer could not be ranked fairly.
feature.races.faq5q: Can someone without an account watch the race?
feature.races.faq5a: No. The link is public and generates a preview if the race is public, but to see the race —and to compete— you need to sign in. It is free.
feature.races.faq6q: Can I lock my phone while I run?
feature.races.faq6a: Not in a race yet: tracking needs the app in the foreground, though the screen stays on by itself. To run with the phone in your pocket, use {{link}}.

feature.challenges.heroLead: A challenge is a goal with a deadline: you pick what gets measured, how long it runs, and that is it. From there the board fills itself with what you train, without logging anything extra.

feature.challenges.met2Counts: The longest run of consecutive training days inside the window.

feature.challenges.met4Counts: Your saved personal best, not just the one from the window.
feature.challenges.met5Counts: Your saved personal best, not just the one from the window.

feature.challenges.score3Title: The last day counts in full
feature.challenges.score3Desc: The window runs from midnight on the opening day to the end of the closing day, in your own time. Nobody loses the last evening for living in another time zone.

feature.challenges.faq4a: From the web version. On your phone you can see your challenges and the days they have left, and everything you train counts the same; to see the leaderboard, for now, come in from the browser.
feature.challenges.faq5q: Do I have to log anything separately?
feature.challenges.faq5a: No. The challenge reads your workouts and your sets exactly as you record them. The only exception is the metric you invent yourself, which is on you.
feature.challenges.faq6a: The challenge moves to your finished ones with the result, and stays there as the record of what you set out to do. Creating the next one takes two minutes.
feature.community.name: Community
feature.community.card: Friends, activity feed, reactions, a weekly leaderboard and blocking and reporting tools.
feature.community.metaTitle: Community: train with friends, not with strangers
feature.community.metaDesc: Follow your friends, react to their workouts and compete on a small board. With blocking, reporting and notification control — and entirely optional.
feature.community.h1: Someone who notices when you show up
feature.community.heroLead: Follow the people who train alongside you, react to what they do and compete on a small board where finishing first actually means something. And if you would rather train alone, nothing breaks: follow nobody and the app works exactly the same.

feature.community.see3What: The workouts and cardio sessions you complete

feature.community.feed1Desc: The workouts and cardio sessions of the people you follow, with what they did and how long ago. And yours, so you see exactly what they see.
feature.community.feed2Desc: Five reactions, one tap: fire, biceps, applause, target and trophy. You can leave several different ones on the same post, and you can see who reacted.
feature.community.feed3Desc: Up to five hundred characters, with replies and with reactions on the comments themselves. Enough to trash-talk, short enough not to become something else.

feature.community.lbLead: Because not everyone is competing for the same thing.

feature.community.lb2Means: Everything you have piled up since you started.
feature.community.lb3Means: The days in a row you have been training.

feature.community.lb5Means: The points you collect along the way.

feature.community.modLead: Two tools, and both of them actually do something instead of just hiding things from your screen.
feature.community.block1: You both stop following each other, and nobody gets told.
feature.community.block2: That person disappears from your feed and you from theirs.
feature.community.block3: Your workouts and your stats stop being readable for them: it is not a screen filter, it is a server rule.
feature.community.block4: Any notifications between the two of you are deleted, in both directions.
feature.community.block5: If you change your mind, unblocking undoes it. Your blocked list is always one tap away.
feature.community.report1: A person or a specific comment, for spam, harassment, inappropriate content or something else, with a written detail if you want.
feature.community.report2: A copy of the reported text is stored, so the review still works even if the comment is deleted afterwards.
feature.community.report3: Reporting the same thing twice does not count twice: the report was already filed.
feature.community.modLimit: We review reports by hand: there is no automated moderation and you will not get a reply with the outcome. If something is urgent or serious, write to us directly instead of waiting.
feature.community.notifLead: They are built to nudge, not to interrupt.
feature.community.notif2: When someone reacts to or comments on something of yours, and when someone replies to your comment.
feature.community.notif4: When you break a record or cross a streak that matters.
feature.community.notif5: When someone you follow trains — once a day, not once per session.
feature.community.notifControl: Each of those groups can be switched off on its own from settings, and there is a master switch to silence everything at once.
feature.community.notifLimit: Outside the app they arrive as system notifications on Android and browser notifications on the web, if you allow them. Without permission they still show up inside the app.

feature.offline.name: Offline and in sync
feature.offline.card: Opens with no signal, keeps the session you are doing and picks it up across Android and the web on the same account.
feature.offline.metaTitle: Train offline, sync when you're back
feature.offline.metaDesc: The app opens with no signal, your session keeps working and picks up on the other device at the exact set. And we say what needs a connection.
feature.offline.h1: No signal in the basement. No excuses.
feature.offline.heroLead: The app opens even with no data, the session you are doing keeps working in full, and if you close it and come back — or switch devices — you land on the same set. Whatever can be uploaded goes up on its own the moment there is a connection.
feature.offline.heroBadge: The session holds for 24 h · picks up on the other device · same account
feature.offline.heroAlt: The same workout session open in the browser and on the phone, both on set 3 of 4 and with no signal
feature.offline.mockCaption: The same set on both screens, with no data.
feature.offline.whatEyebrow: The app does not depend on your coverage
feature.offline.whatHeading: What happens with no signal, exactly
feature.offline.whatLead: Every training app says it works offline and none of them explains what that means. Here is what it means, row by row.
feature.offline.what1Offline: It opens the same way, from the copy your device saved the first time.
feature.offline.what1Back: It catches up on its own.
feature.offline.what2Offline: Works in full: the exercises, the timed rests and their alerts.
feature.offline.what2Back: It syncs as soon as there is a connection.
feature.offline.what3Offline: When you come back you are on the same set, up to twenty-four hours later.
feature.offline.what3Back: Same, and the session is also waiting on your other device.
feature.offline.what4Offline: Stored on the device with its route, up to five pending.
feature.offline.what4Back: It uploads itself, with nothing for you to do.
feature.offline.what5Offline: Stored on the device, up to five pending.
feature.offline.what5Back: It uploads itself when the connection returns or when you open the app.
feature.offline.what6Offline: You log them and they stay logged.
feature.offline.what6Back: They upload themselves, even if you edited or deleted them in the meantime.
feature.offline.what7Thing: Your sets and the completed workout
feature.offline.what7Offline: You see them on screen and the session moves on as normal, but saving them to your account needs a connection at that moment.
feature.offline.what7Back: There is no automatic retry: what could not be uploaded is not recorded.
feature.offline.what8Offline: They need a connection, and if the server does not answer the app tells you instead of pretending it saved.
feature.offline.what9Thing: The feed, the leaderboard and challenges
feature.offline.what10Offline: On Android yes: all 1,578 exercises ship inside the app. In the browser the library asks the server for its list, so offline it comes up short.
feature.offline.whatLimit: Row seven is the one nobody tells you about, so we will: training with no coverage works and anything you finish — cardio, circuits and water — uploads itself, but strength sets get no retry. If you are going to train underground, count on the detail of that session possibly not being saved. We would rather tell you here than let you find out on day one.
feature.offline.syncTitle: Start on the computer, finish on the phone
feature.offline.syncLead: Nothing to export, no devices to pair and no starting over.
feature.offline.sync1Desc: You open the workout of the day on the computer, on the big screen, or straight on the phone if you are already at the park.
feature.offline.sync2Title: Every set is saved right away
feature.offline.sync2Desc: What you tick is stored on the device instantly and travels to your account every fifteen seconds, without you pressing save anywhere.
feature.offline.sync3Title: You carry on on the other screen
feature.offline.sync3Desc: You open the app on your phone and you are on the same set, with the same rest and the same elapsed time. No hunting for where you left off.
feature.offline.syncNote: It does not matter which screen you start {{link}} on: it is the same account on both sides, nothing to export, import or migrate, and the session waits for you for up to twenty-four hours.
feature.offline.instLead: You can use both at once: that is what most people do.
feature.offline.inst1Desc: It downloads straight from this site, with its version, its size and its date in plain sight. And {{link}} travels inside it: all 1,578 exercises can be searched with no data.
feature.offline.inst2Desc: It runs in any modern browser and you can add it to your home screen so it opens full screen, like any other app. Updates ask before they apply, so none of them will interrupt you halfway through a workout.
feature.offline.instLimit: There is still no native iPhone app. You use the web version from Safari, which can also be added to the home screen and also opens offline.
feature.offline.platTitle: What you can do on each one
feature.offline.platLead: Almost everything works the same on both. The two real differences are the offline exercise library and reminders with everything closed, and both favour the Android app.
feature.offline.plat2: Install it on your home screen
feature.offline.plat3: Keep the session you are doing even if you close it
feature.offline.plat4: Pick it up on the other device

feature.offline.plat8: Reminders with the app and the browser closed

feature.offline.faq1q: Do I lose the workout if the app closes?
feature.offline.faq1a: No. The session in progress is saved to the device at every step and, when you open it again, you are on the same set up to twenty-four hours later. You can even carry on from the other device.
feature.offline.faq2q: Can I train with no coverage?
feature.offline.faq2a: Yes: the app opens and the session works in full, with its rests and its alerts. What needs a connection is saving the detail of your sets to your account, and that is not retried afterwards. Better to know it before you head down to the basement than to find out on the way out.
feature.offline.faq3q: What uploads itself when the connection is back?
feature.offline.faq3a: The cardio outings and circuits you finished with no signal — up to five of each — and the glasses of water you logged. They are stored on the device and sent the moment there is a connection, with nothing for you to do.
feature.offline.faq4a: No. The Android app downloads straight from this site, with its version, its size and its date in plain sight, and the browser version runs in any modern browser without installing anything.
feature.offline.faq5a: There is no native iOS app yet. You can use the web version from Safari and install it to your home screen: it opens full screen and it also works offline.
feature.offline.faq6q: Do I have to move my data from one device to the other?
feature.offline.faq6a: No. It is the same account on both sides: nothing to export, import or pair.
